title: In the AI era, every company ends up a generative system company, and the middleman gets killed
dek: Internet platforms exploit the production side through their power of distribution: the same content gets different reach depending on who posts it, which shows the distribution mechanism has failed. Generative systems internalize distribution, connecting demand and production directly — production and consumption become one.
why: Wang Guan uses a three-part data framework to reason through the survival path of AI application companies; the second half, on generative systems, prosumers and the shift in platform power, is the densest part.
who: AI application-layer founders, product managers, investors watching the shift in the platform economy — especially those thinking about the boundary between application companies and model companies.
skip: 2:00-28:00 personal history and early product attempts, can be skipped quickly.

points.h: Data determines the boundary of intelligence; algorithms only determine how much emerges
points.body: Wang Guan imagines intelligence as a circle: the boundary is set by data, compute is the speed at which you approach the boundary, and algorithms are the part that breaks through the boundary to produce emergence. He quotes the industry's self-mockery that ‘however much human labor, that much intelligence’, pointing out that when algorithms can't move the needle, it always ends up being the product manager who goes after data, because data represents an understanding of business knowhow. Technology can trade RL for data, but only if closed domains like code and math can automatically verify quality; the knowhow in a large number of open scenarios can only be converted into data by people.

points.h: The public-data stage is over; the product startup opportunity is in the third data
points.body: Wang Guan divides data into three stages: the public-data stage is about who reaches the fixed boundary first, suited to organizations with high talent density, ample compute and fast decisions; the domain-data stage is about ‘I have it and you don't’, favoring big companies and traditional industries with good IT; the third is product-endogenous data, data that didn't exist before and only arises because you designed the product form. ChatGPT is the sample — the data of conversation solving all kinds of problems didn't exist historically, and it built its moat by creating new data. Application companies must design, from day one, a new kind of data that can be trained back into the model.

points.h: The data flywheel is an inaccurate term; you have to filter for data above the model's level
points.body: Wang Guan thinks the term ‘data flywheel’ is inaccurate, because not all data is useful. If you train all user data back without filtering, the model's capability will converge toward the average intelligence level of all users, and may even get dumber. He mentions that the data FSD can use for training today may already be less than one thousandth, and it certainly wasn't like that at the start — the filtering standard kept being raised. The core principle is to find, in existing data, the part that adds to wisdom; you have to learn from people smarter than you.

points.h: The boundary between model companies and application companies is disappearing
points.body: Wang Guan thinks we shouldn't distinguish model companies from application companies today: model companies have all started doing products, and application companies shouldn't be seen as shells either, but as companies that haven't started building their own models yet. Cursor has always been building its own models; only by holding the base model in your own hands can costs be controlled and profit actually generated. Application companies will hit the capability boundary of the base model, because the base is general, its parameter count is fixed, and capability allocated across different tasks — some promote each other, some are mutually exclusive.

points.h: A generative system is a method, not a specific product
points.body: Wang Guan analogizes the generative system to the recommendation system: the recommendation system is a technical method that can turn recommending articles into Jinri Toutiao, and recommending videos into Douyin. The generative system consists of three parts: the DSL defines how the problem is accurately expressed; the Context layer reduces the entropy of user intent and the entropy of agent action; the Environment is the interface where humans and agents act together, and needs a reward function to filter effective data. He stresses that the Agent vs. Workflow debate doesn't exist internally — both are essentially about producing more effective Context.

points.h: The generative system kills the middleman; there is no distribution step
points.body: Wang Guan says the essential difference between the generative system and the recommendation system is ‘no middleman taking a cut’ — all internet platforms are middlemen. He gives a thought experiment: suppose two people have identical user profiles, post the same content at the same time and place, and still get different reach, because their identity weights differ — which shows the distribution mechanism has failed. The generative system internalizes distribution: the user's demand for content goes directly to the production side, and the production side generates content directly for the user, shifting from an inventory-allocation logic to a direct-order logic.

points.h: The north star metric is the degree of intelligence, not the number of users
points.body: Wang Guan says there's no doubt that doing products has commercial value, but above that you should measure by the intelligence of the whole system. Intelligence has two dimensions: under the same input, being able to produce higher-scoring content; and for the same quality of content, the fewer tokens consumed the more intelligent. He uses doing a problem as an analogy: one person looks at the problem once and gives the answer directly, another works at it for ages, gets it wrong, starts over, and finally both are right — the former is smarter. So he values a small number of users generating massive revenue more than a massive number of users generating the same revenue.

points.h: The future produces IP; the currency shifts from attention to trust
points.body: Wang Guan reasons that future producers won't produce single-point content, but continuous content with shared attributes abstracted into a Recipe, which he calls IP. The currency of the economic system will change too: previously it was attention, which is why you get content that's unreadable for two or three seconds, looping, gaming the recommendation algorithm. But when content supply is excessive and attention is limited, value shifts to trust. He gives the example of ‘Blizzard出品必属精品’ — though Blizzard is not what it was today, in earlier years that phrase represented trust.

terms.def: A structured language designed for a specific problem, between natural language and code.
Wang Guan borrows concepts from cognitive science: System 1 is the model's instinctive reaction, System 2 is the construction of Context outside the model.
Designing effective Context outside the base model to make the model output better results.
Producing while consuming; the production process itself has value for the producer.
The mechanism for evaluating and filtering effective data, which determines what the system reinforces.

quotes.text: No middleman taking a cut. Who is the middleman now? The middleman now — actually all internet platforms are middlemen.
The capability of your model will converge toward the average intelligence level of all the users using it.
Today's application companies — we shouldn't just see them as so-called shells, or software companies, app companies, but as companies that haven't started building their own models yet.
The same product has a different price. So why can the generative system do better? Because there's no this step — there's no distribution step.

Using a small number of users — I use three users to generate 1 million in revenue, versus using 100,000 users to generate 1 million in revenue — you'd say, for your company, right? For us we'd value the former more.
